traveler: Hylas, pantomime dancer of Augustan Rome
title: The Pupil Brought Up to a Contest of Equality: Hylas, the Divided Benches, and the Open Atrium
years: fl. c. 20 BCE - c. 10 BCE (birth, birthplace and death all unrecorded)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Salmacis, or the Name Before Rome

stops.name: Salmacis, the spring that may be his
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No ancient source gives Hylas a birthplace. The only warrant is the inscription CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197, in which the pantomime Theoros boasts of victory over Hylas of Salmacis; whether that Hylas is Pylades's pupil is an unproven modern identification, since Hylas was a reusable stage name and the stone does not call its Hylas anyone's pupil. The date is arbitrary and orders the segment only. Pin inherited byte-identical from herodotus.journey.json, the atlas's Halicarnassus.
stops.campa: Beside Halicarnassus a spring runs under the name Salmacis, and the Carian coast sends its dancers, its singers and its boys west along the sea lanes to Rome. One inscription, cut for another man's victory, calls a defeated pantomime Hylas of Salmacis. Nothing else in the ancient record gives the dancer a country. He may have been born within a morning's walk of this water; he may never have seen it. The stone that carries the name was paid for by Theoros to list the men he had beaten; it was not cut to tell anyone anything about Hylas.
suggested_refs: The spring and quarter of Salmacis at Halicarnassus, modern Bodrum
CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197, the Theoros victory inscription
sources: Theatrum lexicon, entries on Theoros and Hylas (theatrum.de/2670, theatrum.de/2672)
Hall and Wyles, eds., New Directions in Ancient Pantomime (Oxford, 2008), cited at second hand

stops.name: Salmacis, the stage name and the boy it belonged to
stops.date_confidence: Interpretive. That imperial pantomimes repeatedly bore mythological names (Pylades, Bathyllus, Paris, Hylas) is a modern observation, chiefly Edith Hall's, not consulted directly this session; no ancient source states that Hylas was a stage name rather than a given one. Date arbitrary. The mythological Hylas of the poets is a wholly distinct figure and is named here only as the source of the word.
stops.campa: The imperial stage runs on borrowed names. Pylades, Bathyllus, Paris, Hylas: dancers take the names of figures out of the poets, and the crowd learns to shout a myth when it means a man. Hylas in the poets is the boy Heracles loses at a spring, pulled under by nymphs who wanted him. Whether the dancer is given the name at birth or takes it when he begins to work, no source says. The dancers he will work among carry the same kind of name, and he will spend his life becoming other people in front of Romans under one of them. No ancient writer remarks on the practice at all; the pattern in the names is something modern scholarship noticed later.
suggested_refs: The convention of mythological stage names among imperial pantomimes
sources: Hall and Wyles, eds., New Directions in Ancient Pantomime (Oxford, 2008), cited at second hand
Juvenal, Satires 1.164, for the mythological Hylas, not re-verified this session

stops.name: Tibur, a rival's victory list
stops.date_confidence: Undated. CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197 is placed by modern scholarship in the late first century BCE or the first century CE; the date here is arbitrary. Findspot disputed and left so: the CIL VI number assigns the stone to Rome, while the Theatrum lexicon calls it a grave inscription from Tibur, and the epigraphic database that might settle it (EDCS, moved from db.edcs.eu to edcs.hist.uzh.ch) could not be reached. Earlier descriptions of the object as a terracotta piece found near Rome are unsupported in the source actually consulted, and the praenomen Gaius for Theoros is unverified.
stops.campa: A pantomime named Theoros has his boast cut in stone: he beat four men, and he names all four, so that their names carry his own. Pylades of Cilicia. Nomius of Syria. Pierus of Tibur. Hylas of Salmacis. It is the nearest thing to a professional register the art leaves behind, and it survives because a winner paid for it. Where the stone lay before it was catalogued is disputed: Rome by its CIL number, Tibur by the lexicon that describes it. Nobody can say for certain that its Hylas is the dancer Pylades taught.
stops.quote: Pylades aus Kilikien, Nomius aus Syrien, Pierus aus Tibur und Hylas aus Salamakis
stops.quote_source: Theatrum lexicon, entry on Theoros, summarizing CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197
suggested_refs: CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197; cf. E. Courtney, Musa Lapidaria, no. 122
The Theoriani, Theoros's supporters' club at Pompeii, CIL IV 1891 and 1917
sources: Theatrum lexicon (theatrum.de/2670)
CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197, not independently verified against an epigraphic database

stops.name: Rome, the Campus Martius: taken as a pupil
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a fact, undated. Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12, writing in the early fifth century CE, some four hundred years after the events, says only that Pylades was famous in his art in the time of Augustus and brought his pupil Hylas up to a contest of equality. The date is a loose placement inside Augustus's reign, 27 BCE to 14 CE. No school, address or teaching site is named anywhere; the pin marks the Campus Martius theatre quarter and is not an attested location.
stops.campa: Pylades of Cilicia is the most famous body in Rome, and he takes a pupil. The training of a pantomime is training in silence: the dancer never speaks, the chorus carries the words, and everything the audience will understand has to arrive through an arm or the tilt of a masked face. Pylades teaches him all of it. Macrobius, writing four centuries later with the story already polished by retelling, says the master brought him along to a contest of equality. He does not say the master meant to.
stops.quote: Hylam discipulum usque ad aequalitatis contentionem eruditione provexit.
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7, the only connected ancient account of Hylas's career
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12 (Latin text via the Internet Archive scan of Jan's edition; Penelope/Thayer)

stops.name: Rome, the people divide
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated. Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13, states the division of popular favour in a single sentence and gives no year; the placement is arbitrary and orders the sequence. Canonical Rome pin, inherited byte-identical from virgil.journey.json.
stops.campa: The pupil comes level with the master, and the city takes sides. Macrobius puts it in one sentence: the people then were divided in their support between the two. Rome already divides itself over chariot colours and over gladiators; now it divides over two men who do not speak. Neither of them has yet done anything the emperor is obliged to notice. Partisans of Pylades and partisans of Hylas fill the same benches, watch the same arm rise, and disagree about what it meant.
stops.quote: Populus deinde inter utriusque suffragia divisus est.
suggested_refs: The factional organisation of Roman theatre audiences under Augustus
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13

stops.name: Rome, what a pantomime is
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, describing the art rather than a dated event; the date orders the segment. The technical account of imperial pantomime (a masked solo dancer taking all roles, a sung libretto, instrumental accompaniment) rests on modern scholarship, chiefly E. J. Jory and the essays in Hall and Wyles, eds., New Directions in Ancient Pantomime, neither consulted directly this session. No ancient source describes Hylas's own technique.
stops.campa: One dancer, masked, takes every part in the piece. A singer or a chorus carries the text, pipes and the scabellum keep the time, and the dancer changes person by changing shape: Agamemnon, then Clytemnestra, then the herald, without a word and without leaving the floor. The mask has no moving mouth, so the hands do the speaking, and Roman audiences learn to read hands the way other audiences read faces. It is an instrument fine enough that two men can fight in public over one gesture. No ancient writer describes how Hylas in particular moved; what is known is the art, not his handling of it. This is the instrument Pylades hands to him.
suggested_refs: E. J. Jory, 'The Literary Evidence for the Beginnings of Imperial Pantomime', BICS 28 (1981)
Ismene Lada-Richards, Silent Eloquence (2007)
sources: Modern scholarship on imperial pantomime, cited at second hand and flagged as such

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, the canticum of Agamemnon
stops.date_confidence: The episode is attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13; the date is arbitrary and orders the segment. No source names a venue for any performance of Hylas: the Theatre of Pompey is used as Rome's principal permanent stone theatre in this period, and the pin is inherited byte-identical from julius_caesar.journey.json, which places the Curia of the same complex. The Greek clausula of the song was garbled by OCR in the full-text scan consulted and is reported here from the Penelope/Thayer text.
stops.campa: Hylas dances a piece that ends on the words the great Agamemnon. To show greatness he shows size: he measures out something lofty and huge, an arm sweeping the height and the breadth of a king, and the crowd sees a big man. It is the obvious reading, and a body trained by Pylades is equipped to deliver it, because Pylades taught him how to make a shape fill a theatre. The Greek word under his feet is megas, and megas can be measured or it can be meant.
suggested_refs: The auditorium of the Theatre of Pompey, whose curve survives in the line of Via di Grotta Pinta
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, the shout from the benches
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13. The date is a sequencing device within the same occasion, not a claim of a second day. Same venue caveat as the previous stop; no source names the theatre. The Greek wording is taken from the Penelope/Thayer text, the OCR scan otherwise consulted having corrupted the Greek letters.
stops.campa: Pylades is in the audience, not on the floor, and he does not wait for the piece to end. The master has come to watch the pupil, and he judges him in public, in the language of the art, on the evidence of one gesture. Rome is used to hearing performers heckled from the benches; what it hears this time is the crowd's own argument settled by the man who taught the dancer on the floor. He calls out in Greek, across the theatre, so that everyone gets it: you are making him tall, not great.
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13-14, the Agamemnon exchange entire
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13, Penelope/Thayer text

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, the crowd makes the master dance
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.14, as the continuation of the same occasion; undated, and the venue is unnamed in the source. Date is a sequencing device. Pin as in the two previous stops.
stops.campa: The audience will not let the criticism stand as words. They force Pylades onto the floor to dance the same piece himself, and at the line he had faulted he measures nothing at all. He shows Agamemnon thinking. Nothing, he holds, suits a great commander better than to think on behalf of everyone. Within the hour the same benches have watched two definitions of greatness danced against each other. Macrobius reports no verdict from the crowd; he reports only what the master did with the line.
stops.quote: Tunc eum populus coegit idem saltare canticum cumque ad locum venisset quem reprehenderat, expressit cogitantem, nihil magis ratus magno duci convenire quam pro omnibus cogitare.
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.14
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.14

stops.name: Rome, the language of the correction
stops.date_confidence: Interpretive. That the exchange is reported in Greek is attested in Macrobius; what that implies about the language of the sung libretto, or about Hylas's own first language, is inference and is attested nowhere. The reading given here follows E. J. Jory, not consulted directly this session. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin, inherited from virgil.journey.json.
stops.campa: Master and pupil quarrel in Greek in a Roman theatre, and the crowd follows the quarrel. The piece ends on a Greek phrase; the correction comes in Greek; the reply to the emperor, when it comes, will be in Greek too. Scholars have read this as evidence that the meaning had to arrive through the body whatever tongue the chorus was singing, since a gesture is legible to everyone in the benches and a sung clause is not. None of it settles where Hylas was born, or whether he had Greek before he had Latin, or what tongue the chorus behind him was singing in.
suggested_refs: E. J. Jory, 'Pylades, Pantomime, and the Preservation of Tragedy', Mediterranean Archaeology 17 (2004)
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13-19, for the Greek of the exchanges
E. J. Jory, cited at second hand

stops.name: Theatre of Marcellus, Hylas dances Oedipus
stops.date_confidence: The episode is attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.15, and is undated; the date orders the segment. Venue not named in any source; the Theatre of Marcellus stands in for a second Augustan theatre and is not evidenced for this performance. Macrobius says only that Pylades rebuked the dancer's securitas, his assurance, with the cry You are looking. He never mentions blindness, never says Hylas moved too confidently for a blind man, and never specifies which episode of the story was danced. The blind-Oedipus reading is a modern inference, plausible but not attested.
stops.campa: Hylas dances Oedipus. What text, what episode, what the piece was called, nobody records. Pylades watches again, and again he corrects him from the benches, in two Greek words: you are looking. Macrobius says the target was the dancer's securitas, his unconcern, the ease of a body moving as though nothing in the world were hidden from it. Later readers have supplied the obvious completion, that a blinded Oedipus should not move like a man who can see. Macrobius does not supply it.
stops.quote: Saltabat Hylas Oedipodem, et Pylades hac voce securitatem saltantis castigavit: Σὺ βλέπεις.
suggested_refs: The Theatre of Marcellus, dedicated 13 or 11 BCE, still standing on the Campus Martius
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.15, Latin text at la.wikisource.org/wiki/Saturnalia/II

stops.name: Rome, the two words that survive him
stops.date_confidence: A reflective stop on the state of the record, placed at the canonical Rome pin and dated only to order the segment. The two Greek exclamations and the Latin frames around them are attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13-15; the assessment of the record's shape is the compiler's, not a source claim.
stops.campa: Of everything Hylas did in his working life, four sentences survive, and in three of them he is being corrected. His own voice is not in the record at all, because his art had no voice and because nobody thought to write down what he said offstage. What Rome kept of him is the shape of two arguments about how a body should mean something. The pupil measures; the master thinks. The pupil sees; the blind man should not. Nothing records what Hylas said to either correction, or whether he said anything.
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12-19, the whole of the surviving narrative
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12-19

stops.name: Rome, the librettos nobody kept
stops.date_confidence: Statement of a gap rather than an event; the date orders the segment. No libretto of an imperial pantomime survives complete, and no ancient source gives a title for the Oedipus or the Agamemnon piece Hylas danced. Assessed from the primary sources reviewed and from the absence noted in modern scholarship on the genre.
stops.campa: Two pieces from his repertoire are named by their content and by nothing else. An Agamemnon, ending on the great Agamemnon. An Oedipus. Rome copied and recopied its tragedies and its epics for centuries and did not copy the words its dancers moved to, because those words were understood to be scaffolding for a body, and the body was the work. The art filled the theatres of the capital for four hundred years, and what survives of it is other people's descriptions of watching it. Not one imperial pantomime libretto survives complete.
suggested_refs: The lost genre of the pantomime libretto, or fabula saltica
sources: Assessed from Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7, and from modern scholarship on the genre cited at second hand

stops.name: Circus Flaminius, the quarrel leaves the theatre
stops.date_confidence: Attested that a populi seditio arose from the contention held between Pylades and Hylas: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19. Undated, and no site is given; the date is arbitrary. The pin marks the Circus Flaminius at the southern end of the Campus Martius, between the Tiber and the Porticus Octaviae, hemmed in on the east by the Theatre of Marcellus. It is an area of public assembly beside the theatres, not an attested location for any disturbance.
stops.campa: The argument about how to dance Agamemnon becomes an argument in the streets. Macrobius calls it a populi seditio, a rising of the people, and traces it directly to the contention held between Pylades and Hylas. Rome's theatre crowds are organised enough to riot and practised enough to do it well; the same benches that divided over a gesture now divide over everything that follows from having taken a side. He gives the whole disturbance one clause, with no date, no site, and no account of what was actually done in the streets.
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19
The Circus Flaminius and the theatre quarter of the southern Campus Martius
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19

stops.name: Palatine, the emperor's anger
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19: Augustus's roused indignation over the riot, and Pylades's reply. Undated; the date orders the segment. Macrobius does not say where the exchange took place, and the Palatine is used as Augustus's residence, a plausible but unattested setting; the pin is inherited from virgil.journey.json. The Greek is verified from Jan's edition. The widely quoted English gloss about the people's spare time belongs to Cassius Dio's separate version, not to this passage, and the two must be quoted apart.
stops.campa: The riot reaches Augustus and the emperor's anger falls on Pylades. Pylades answers him in Greek, and the answer is not an apology: you are ungrateful, king; let them busy themselves about us. The princeps who has spent twenty years converting a republic's attention into his own has just been told by a dancer what the dancers are for. Macrobius records no reprisal in this sentence. Suetonius, in another book and without saying the incidents are connected, records that Augustus had Hylas flogged and Pylades put out of Italy.
stops.quote: Καὶ ἀχαριστεῖς, βασιλεῦ· ἔασον αὐτοὺς περὶ ἡμᾶς ἀσχολεῖσθαι.
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19
Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, for the punishments
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19 (Jan's edition, archive.org bub_gb_IjNCAAAAIAAJ, p. 256)
Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4

stops.name: Rome, the theatres under watch
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Augustus punished performers personally and publicly: one passage of Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, records the flogging of Hylas, the whipping of the actor Stephanio through all three theatres and his banishment, and the expulsion of Pylades from Rome and from Italy. Suetonius gives no date for any of the three and does not state that they are connected; the date here is arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Suetonius puts three punishments in one breath. The actor Stephanio, who let a married woman dressed as a boy wait on him, is whipped through all three theatres and then sent away. Pylades is thrown out of Rome and out of Italy for pointing his finger at a spectator who had hissed him, turning the whole house on the man. Hylas is flogged in his own atrium. The emperor who let the crowds keep their dancers also kept a list. Suetonius does not say the three cases had anything to do with each other.
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, on Augustus's discipline of performers
sources: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, via LacusCurtius and en.wikisource.org (Thomson translation)

stops.name: Roman Forum, a praetor lodges a complaint
stops.date_confidence: Attested that a praetor complained and that the complaint reached Augustus: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4. Undated; no charge, hearing, evidence or outcome is recorded, and the praetor is not named. The Forum, ordinary seat of praetorian judicial business, is a plausible but unattested setting; the pin is the canonical Rome pin, inherited byte-identical from virgil.journey.json.
stops.campa: A praetor complains about Hylas. Suetonius does not say what the complaint was, does not name the praetor, does not report a hearing, and does not say whether anything was proved. One of Rome's senior magistrates, a man with his own tribunal and his own jurisdiction, takes a grievance against a dancer past his own court and lays it in front of the princeps instead. Why he wanted the princeps to hear it rather than his own tribunal, Suetonius never says.
suggested_refs: The praetorian tribunals of the Roman Forum
sources: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4

stops.name: Rome, the house of Hylas
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Hylas had a house with an atrium: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4. Nothing else about it is recorded and no source says where in Rome it stood; the coordinates mark a generic point in the theatre quarter and are not an address. Whether Hylas was freeborn, enslaved or freed is nowhere stated, so the legal standing of the house and of the man in it is unknown. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: He has a house, and the house has an atrium. That is the whole of what is known about how Hylas lived. Whether he was born free, born a slave, or freed, no source says, and the atrium does not settle it, because freedmen built atria too. An atrium is the room a Roman household keeps for being seen in: the light drops through the roof onto the pool, the clients wait there in the morning, the masks of the ancestors hang along the walls of a family that has them.
suggested_refs: The Roman atrium as the household's public room
sources: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4

stops.name: Rome, flogged in his own atrium
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the flogging, its location in Hylas's own atrium, and its deliberate visibility (nemine excluso) are all in Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, the earliest and only near-contemporary notice naming Hylas. Undated. The Latin quoted is a subordinate clause governed by coercuit, hence the perfect subjunctive verberarit; many modern quotations silently print verberavit. Not recorded: the charge, guilt, the number of blows, injuries, or any connection to the riot.
stops.campa: Augustus orders him whipped, orders it done in his own atrium, and orders that nobody be shut out. The room built for a household to be looked at is used to look at the household's owner being beaten. It is not carried out in a prison or a barracks or the street; it is carried out at the exact place where a Roman keeps his standing, in front of anyone who cares to walk in. Suetonius gives the whole business eleven words and never says what Hylas had done.
stops.quote: Hylan pantomimum querente praetore in atrio domus suae nemine excluso flagellis verberarit.
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, the only near-contemporary notice of Hylas
sources: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, Latin at thelatinlibrary.com/suetonius/suet.aug.html

stops.name: Rome, nemine excluso
stops.date_confidence: The same attested event as the previous stop, held for a second look; the date is a sequencing device and not a claim of a second day. The phrase nemine excluso is Suetonius's; the reading of it as the point of the sentence is interpretation. Rolfe's Loeb rendering (1913), quoted here, is the standard English.
stops.campa: Two words carry the sentence: nemine excluso, nobody excluded. The emperor could have had the man flogged anywhere. He chose the one room in Rome whose whole purpose is publicity, and then took the door out of it. Rolfe's Loeb gives the phrase as publicly scourged, which is accurate and which loses the arrangement in the Latin, where the doors are not opened but unclosed. The crowds that had divided over Hylas are free to walk in off the street and watch it done.
stops.quote: Hylas, a pantomimic actor, was publicly scourged in the atrium of his own house, on complaint of a praetor.
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45, trans. J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library (1913), via LacusCurtius
suggested_refs: J. C. Rolfe's Loeb translation of the Divus Augustus, still the standard English
sources: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, Rolfe translation via penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, after
stops.date_confidence: Gap, stated as such. No ancient source records anything about Hylas after the notices in Suetonius and Macrobius: no later performance, no retirement, no exile, no death, no burial, no tomb. Assessed from the primary sources reviewed. The date is arbitrary and closes the segment.
stops.campa: And then nothing. No source records whether he danced again, whether he stayed in Rome, whether he was ruined, whether he was forgiven, whether he lived another year or another thirty. A man whose art was the most watched thing in the city leaves a record that stops in the middle of a whipping. The silence after it is not a lost document; it is the ordinary shape of the evidence for performers, who are written about by senators or not at all. There is no death notice, no tomb, no epitaph, no year.
suggested_refs: The absence of any death notice or burial for the dancer Hylas
sources: Assessed from Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, and Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12-19

segments.name: What the Sources Do Not Say

stops.name: Rome, no name, no parents, no status
stops.date_confidence: Gap. No ancient source records Hylas's birth name, birth date, birthplace independent of the disputed Salmacis inscription, parents, legal status, owner or patron, spouse, or children. Assessed from Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, Cassius Dio 54.17.4-5, and Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12-19. The date is arbitrary and orders the segment.
stops.campa: What is not known about Hylas: when he was born, where, to whom, under what name, free or unfree, owned by anyone, freed by anyone, married, childless or not, how he was paid and by whom, what he was worth, what he looked like out of the mask. What is known: that Pylades taught him, that he danced an Agamemnon and an Oedipus, that Rome divided its favour over him, that the division ended in a riot, and that a praetor complained and the emperor had him whipped at home with the doors open.
suggested_refs: The prosopography of imperial performers, in which Hylas appears without status or family
sources: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4
Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12-19
Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4-5

stops.name: Rome, no contract, no portrait
stops.date_confidence: Gap. No papyrus, contract, libretto manuscript, letter, household record, legal dossier or securely labelled portrait of the dancer Hylas has been identified by modern scholarship, and nothing of the kind surfaced in the searching done for this file. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Nothing of him is an object. No contract, no receipt, no letter, no household ledger, no roll of a libretto with his name in the margin, no bust with a caption, no mask kept anywhere. The imperial theatre produced enormous quantities of paper and stone about itself, and none of it is his. What circulates today under the name Hylas shows either a different man of the same name or a boy out of a poem, and the museums holding those things have never claimed the dancer for them. A search for an object with his name on it returns the myth and the homonyms, and stops there.
suggested_refs: The absence of any securely labelled ancient portrait of the dancer Hylas
sources: Assessed as a gap; searches of Wikipedia and general search engines returned only mythological and homonymous material

stops.name: Rome, the four-hundred-year gap
stops.date_confidence: Assessment of the record, not a dated event; the date is arbitrary. Suetonius wrote around 121 CE, roughly a century after Hylas; Macrobius, the only connected narrative source for the artistic career, wrote in the early fifth century CE, some four hundred years later. Whether Macrobius drew on a good Augustan source or on a school tradition polished by retelling cannot be determined from the text.
stops.campa: Everything told about Hylas's art comes from one chapter of a book written four hundred years after him, staged at a dinner party that never happened, by a man collecting good stories about the old theatre. Macrobius did not see Hylas dance and neither did anybody he could have asked. The anecdotes have the shape anecdotes acquire in transmission: two exchanges, both witty, both won by the master. That does not make them false. It means the pupil's side of the record was edited by people who preferred the master.
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 2, and the tradition of theatrical anecdote it collects
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7
Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4

stops.name: Rome, the columbarium of another Hylas
stops.date_confidence: An attested monument belonging to the wrong man. The columbarium just outside the Porta Latina was built roughly 14-54 CE, dated by niches for a freedman of Tiberius and one of Claudia Octavia, and was bought and redecorated by a freedman named Gnaeus Pomponius Hylas for himself and his wife; Pietro Campana excavated it in 1831. He is not the Augustan dancer, and nothing connects them but the cognomen. Some accounts give the praenomen as Publius and put the tomb on the Via Latina; the mosaic reads CN and the monument stands on the Via di Porta Latina.
stops.campa: Outside the Porta Latina, down a stair cut into the tufa, a small painted chamber holds the ash urns of a freedman's household. Over the door a mosaic in green and white names Gnaeus Pomponius Hylas and his wife Pomponia Vitalinis. Niches inside were cut for a freedman of Tiberius and one of Claudia Octavia, which puts the tomb a generation or two after the dancer. Nothing joins the two men but a Greek cognomen that thousands of freedmen in the city carried. It is one of the few places in Rome where the name Hylas can be read cut in stone. Pietro Campana excavated the chamber in 1831.
stops.quote: CN(aei) POMPONI HYLAE ET POMPONIAE CN(aei) L(ibertae) VITALINIS
stops.quote_source: Mosaic panel over the entrance, Columbarium of Pomponius Hylas, Via di Porta Latina, Rome

stops.name: Rome, the same joke told about another man
stops.date_confidence: A source conflict, dated to Cassius Dio's own composition of the Roman History in the early third century CE rather than to the episode it reports. Dio 54.17.4-5 places Pylades's restoration from exile and his reply to Augustus in 18 BCE by narrative sequence; the consuls Furnius and Silanus, sometimes cited as the anchor, belong to 54.18.1, which opens the following year. Dio's antagonist there is Bathyllus, the favourite of Maecenas, and he never mentions Hylas. Macrobius attaches a reply of the same kind to the Hylas rivalry, in different words. The two traditions conflict; neither is used here to fill the other's gaps.
stops.campa: Cassius Dio tells a version in which Hylas does not appear at all. Pylades is brought back from exile, Augustus reproaches him for quarrelling with Bathyllus of Alexandria, the freedman of Maecenas who founded the other school of the art, and Pylades answers that it suits Caesar for the people to spend their idle hours on dancers. Macrobius tells the same kind of answer with Hylas standing where Bathyllus stands and different words in Pylades's mouth. Modern retellings have merged the two and produced an exile of Hylas that no ancient source reports.
stops.quote: It is to your advantage, Caesar, that the people should devote their spare time to us
stops.quote_source: Pylades to Augustus, Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.5
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4-5, via LacusCurtius
Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19, for the competing version
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4-5
Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19

stops.name: Manchester, the nymphs take the name
stops.date_confidence: Attested: John William Waterhouse painted Hylas and the Nymphs in 1896, and the canvas hangs in Manchester Art Gallery on Mosley Street. The subject is the mythological Hylas, companion of Heracles, and has nothing to do with the dancer. Included as evidence of the modern crowding-out of the name, an assessment borne out by searching that returns myth material and no historical dancer.
stops.campa: Waterhouse paints the boy at the pool with seven nymphs rising out of the water lilies to take him, and the picture becomes one of the most reproduced images in Britain. From that year the word Hylas in English belongs to the myth. The Augustan pantomime who set Rome shouting has no article of his own in any general reference work in any language checked. Search for the dancer and this pool comes up instead, again and again: the water, the pale arms, the mouths just parted.
suggested_refs: J. W. Waterhouse, Hylas and the Nymphs (1896), Manchester Art Gallery
sources: Manchester Art Gallery collection record; Wikipedia, 'Hylas and the Nymphs'

stops.name: Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Loeb Macrobius
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Robert A. Kaster's edition and translation of Macrobius's Saturnalia was published in the Loeb Classical Library by Harvard University Press in 2011; the volume numbers, usually given as 510-512, could not be re-verified this session, the publisher's catalogue page returning an empty response. The pin marks the press, not an ancient site.
stops.campa: The four sentences that preserve Hylas's art pass into English through a Harvard edition in three green volumes. Kaster prints the Latin and the Greek exclamations facing a translation, and a reader who has never heard of the dancer meets him inside a footnote to a fifth-century dinner party. He exists in modern scholarship as a case inside studies of the genre, cited by Jory, by Hall and Wyles, by Lada-Richards, always as an example of something else. There is no biography of Hylas, no monograph, no chapter with his name on it.

stops.name: Rome, the curve of Via di Grotta Pinta
stops.date_confidence: Present-day topography, attested: the buildings around Via di Grotta Pinta preserve the curve of the auditorium of the Theatre of Pompey, and the Theatre of Marcellus survives carrying apartments. That Hylas performed in either building is nowhere attested; no source names a venue for any of his recorded performances. Pin inherited byte-identical from julius_caesar.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Theatre of Pompey is gone and its shape is not. A street off the Campo de' Fiori bends in a long arc because the houses were built into the seating, and a cellar under a restaurant is a wedge of the ancient substructure. A mile off, the Theatre of Marcellus carries three floors of apartments on its arches. Nobody can say which of them Hylas worked in, or whether either. The rooms where a city argued about whether greatness is tall or thoughtful are still standing, and lived in.

The Theatre of Marcellus, Via del Teatro di Marcello
